name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,825

entries.clue: Pilot has relocated, getting better place (8)

indicatorNotes.relocated: Anything relocated has been picked up and set down somewhere else, and these letters move the same way.

blocks.note: eight letters to work from, exactly the count the grid wants

annotation.surface: A pilot who has moved house.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Relocated' sits in the surface as a fact about the pilot's address and is the instruction. The definition is a whole phrase, not a word: somewhere you go to get better.
annotation.definitionFit: A hospital is named here by what happens in it — people are taken there to recover — rather than by any synonym.

entries.clue: Joker 50% down in hustings, pollsters admitted (8)

indicatorNotes.50% down: Down here is the sense a share price is down: cut by 50%, the word beside it keeps only half of its letters.
indicatorNotes.admitted: To be admitted is to be let inside, so the letters named here go within the ones already standing.

blocks.note: the hustings are the public meetings of a British election campaign, and halved the word leaves its first four letters
MORI, now Ipsos MORI, is the polling firm quoted whenever a British opinion poll is reported

annotation.surface: Nobody laughing on the campaign trail as the pollsters are let in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Down' looks like a candidate slipping in the polls and means reduced by half. The pollsters admitted are a named firm, which is the piece to learn.
annotation.definitionFit: A humorist is a professional wit who writes or performs for laughs, which is what a joker does for a living.

entries.clue: Not one large citrus fruit turned white (8)

annotation.definitionNote: 'White' is the wine and not the colour, and the answer is one white grape among many, so the definition names the class it belongs to.

indicatorNotes.turned: To turn a thing is to face it the other way about, so the pieces built up here are read from the far end back.

blocks.note: not one of them and no to them come to the same thing
L is large on a clothing label
limes are citrus, and the plural supplies the five letters needed

annotation.surface: A crate of large citrus fruit in which not one has gone white.
annotation.walkthrough: Semillon is the grape behind white Bordeaux and Sauternes, so the last word of the clue is a noun. 'Turned' is the only word saying the three pieces are read backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Semillon is a white wine grape, and a wine made from it is sold simply as a white.

entries.clue: Antique coins Len traded worth nothing (15)

indicatorNotes.traded: Traded things change hands and end up somewhere other than where they started, which is what becomes of these letters.

blocks.note: fifteen letters, the full width of the grid

annotation.surface: Len swapping old coins that turn out to be worthless.
annotation.walkthrough: Three ordinary words carry all fifteen letters, and Len is in the clue only for his three of them. Swapping and trading are the same act, which is why the instruction reads as part of the story.
annotation.definitionFit: Something inconsequential has no consequences and no weight, so it counts for nothing and is worth nothing to anybody.

entries.clue: Friend's gone across motorway (5)

indicatorNotes.across: A plank laid across a gap spans it from side to side, so the word it applies to opens out and takes the next piece into the middle.

blocks.note: a week gone and a week ago are the same week
the M1 is Britain's first motorway, London to Leeds, and its number is written in the grid as the letter I

annotation.surface: A friend who has crossed the motorway.
annotation.walkthrough: Motorway means MI in a grid, the M1 with its figure written as a letter, and that convention is worth pocketing. 'Gone' looks like part of the friend's story and is a three-letter word for past.
annotation.definitionFit: Amigo is Spanish for friend and has been at home in English since the Westerns, used for a companion or a pal.

entries.clue: Son turning Dutchman out of yard - he's untidy (6)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a sentence about a man rather than a noun, and the answer is the word for the man it describes.

indicatorNotes.turning: To turn somebody out is to put them out, so whatever is named here is evicted rather than kept.
indicatorNotes.out of: Out of names the thing being left behind, so what follows is what loses a piece.

blocks.note: S is son on a family tree
Johan Cruyff, the Netherlands' greatest footballer and later Barcelona's manager
yard shortens to y on a ruler, and it is the letter turned out

annotation.surface: A son evicting a Dutchman from the yard.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface turns the Dutchman out of the yard; the wordplay turns the yard out of the Dutchman. Cruyff is the footballer, and it is his Y that goes.
annotation.definitionFit: A scruff is somebody who looks a mess — unbrushed, unpressed, shirt hanging out — so the untidy man of the clue is one.

entries.clue: Statistician's compared angry Irish band member with happy (5-10)

annotation.definitionNote: The possessive says whose word is wanted: 'compared' is the everyday verb, and the answer is the statistician's version of it.

blocks.note: cross is mildly angry, the word you use to a child
the Corrs are a family band from Dundalk, so one of them is a Corr
elated is happy at its highest pitch

annotation.surface: A statistician weighing a bad-tempered Irish musician against a cheerful one.
annotation.walkthrough: Three plain synonyms stack up with nothing hidden between them, and the band is the only real obstacle. The hyphen falls exactly where the first piece ends.
annotation.definitionFit: To cross-correlate two sets of figures is to measure how far one matches the other, which is comparing them the statistician's way.

entries.clue: Maintenance on battlements? (6)

blocks.note: on the roof and up on the roof put you in the same place
the keep is a castle's central tower, the strong point the battlements run round

annotation.surface: A question about what it costs to look after a castle.
annotation.walkthrough: Split the answer in two and the clue's question answers itself: a man on the battlements is up the keep. The question mark is the setter owning up to how playful the join is.
annotation.definitionFit: Upkeep is the money and labour a building or a vehicle needs to stay in good order, which is its maintenance.

entries.clue: Fellow in a horizontal position doing a Superman impression? (6)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition points at the answer through its most famous instance instead of defining the word, which is what the question mark admits.

blocks.note: F is fellow, as in Fellow of the Royal Society
lying is what you are doing when you are horizontal

annotation.surface: A man stretched out flat on the floor, pretending to be Superman.
annotation.walkthrough: The joke and the wordplay are the same thing: the impression only works lying down. 'Fellow' looks like the man in the picture and is a single letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Superman's whole act is flight, one arm out ahead of him, so anyone doing his impression is flying.

entries.clue: Awful tower had grim cells (5,3)

annotation.definitionNote: Death row is a whole line of cells taken together, so the plural definition names the collection the singular answer stands for.

indicatorNotes.Awful: An awful state of affairs is one where nothing is where it ought to be, and that goes for these letters as well.

blocks.note: eight letters to rearrange, the length wanted

annotation.surface: A dreadful tower that had bleak cells inside it.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface builds a medieval keep and the answer is a modern American prison block. 'Awful' opens the clue in its ordinary sense and is doing the shuffling.
annotation.definitionFit: Death row is the line of cells holding prisoners who are waiting to be executed, which is about as grim as a cell gets.

entries.clue: Act like a woman whose little hand is frozen with cold (5)

blocks.clueFragment: a woman whose little hand is frozen
blocks.note: in Puccini's La Boheme, Rodolfo takes Mimi's hand and sings that it is frozen
C is cold, as marked on a tap

annotation.surface: Behaving like a woman whose small hand has gone numb in the cold.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Your tiny hand is frozen' is the aria Rodolfo sings to Mimi in La Boheme, and it is the only way into the first four letters. The clue describes her rather than naming her.
annotation.definitionFit: To mimic somebody is to copy their voice and their manner, which is acting like them.

entries.clue: Wrong choice crucial in rough game with sticks and blades (3,6)

annotation.definition: rough game with sticks and blades

indicatorNotes.Wrong: A word spelt wrong has the right letters standing in the wrong places, which is the state these letters are in.

blocks.note: six letters to rearrange
the key question is the crucial one

annotation.surface: A bad decision that proved crucial in a violent match.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crucial in rough' reads as one phrase about a hard-fought game, and the definition begins in the middle of it. The blades are skates.
annotation.definitionFit: Ice hockey is played with sticks by men on skate blades, and its checking and fighting have made roughness part of the sport's reputation.

entries.clue: Forbidding university jargon fills tedious course (6,3)

indicatorNotes.fills: Whatever fills a thing is inside it, so the letters named here are poured into the word alongside.

blocks.note: a rut is the dull track a stuck life runs along
U is university, as in the name of any redbrick
lingo is the private vocabulary of a trade or a gang

annotation.surface: University jargon packed into a dull lecture course.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tedious course' looks like the lecture series the jargon fills and is a three-letter word for a groove. 'Forbidding' has to be heard as the verb, not as the adjective meaning stern.
annotation.definitionFit: To rule something out is to forbid it, striking it off the list of what may be done.

entries.clue: Maybe Schmidt drained his one? (5)

indicatorNotes.drained: A drained vessel has had everything between its ends emptied out, so the word keeps only its first and last letters.

blocks.note: SCHMIDT emptied of everything between its first letter and its last
Schmidt being German, his word for one is ein

annotation.surface: A man called Schmidt finishing off his drink.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word works twice: read straight a German has emptied his tankard, read as instructions his name is drained and his 'one' is German. Schmidt is 'maybe' because any German surname would serve.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight the clue is the thing itself: a stein is the heavy German tankard, and Schmidt has drunk his dry.

entries.clue: E.g. press secretary rung by no press after work (12)

annotation.definitionNote: A press secretary is one kind of spokesperson, and the 'e.g.' owns up to the definition naming an example rather than a synonym.

indicatorNotes.after work: Work is the verb here: clay that has been worked comes out in a shape quite unlike the one it went in with, and so do these letters.

blocks.note: a ladder's rung and a wheel's spoke are the same bar, and the words stand in for each other
seven letters to rearrange

annotation.surface: A press secretary who got no calls from reporters once the office had shut.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rung' reads as the past of ring, with the phone in mind, and it is the bar of a ladder. 'After work' completes the office picture and is the instruction to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: A press secretary speaks to the media on a government's or a boss's behalf, which is one job among many held by a spokesperson.

entries.clue: Man in photo with muscles cycles with passengers (8)

indicatorNotes.in: A man in a photograph is inside it, so the letters named before this word go between the letters of the word after it.

blocks.note: a pic is a photo, as in holiday pics
Ed is the crossword's stock short man, from Edward or Edwin
abs are the stomach muscles of the gym

annotation.surface: A photo of a man with a well-developed set of stomach muscles.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a gym selfie and the answer is a taxi. 'Cycles' is the definition's noun, the machines themselves, not a verb about pedalling.
annotation.definitionFit: A pedicab is a bicycle rickshaw, pedalled by its driver with fare-paying passengers in the seat behind.

entries.clue: Brothers brought up unruly, none learning place (8)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition names a kind of place and the answer is one particular institution, the usual licence for a proper noun.

indicatorNotes.brought up: What is brought up travels from the foot of a down entry towards the top, so those letters arrive the other way round.
indicatorNotes.unruly: An unruly crowd will not stay in the order it was put in, and nor will these letters.

blocks.note: brothers shorten to bros, set down here from the bottom of the column upwards
the four letters of none, reordered

annotation.surface: Brothers raised badly, with none of them learning a thing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Brought up' does the work twice over: how the brothers were raised, and an instruction to read upwards. The Sorbonne is the ancient university of Paris, at the heart of the Latin Quarter.
annotation.definitionFit: The Sorbonne has taught in Paris since the thirteenth century and its name stands for the university itself, so it is a place of learning.

entries.clue: American eagle all over American's ID (8)

indicatorNotes.all over: Paint all over a wall covers every part of it, so the letters this applies to close right round the piece that follows.

blocks.note: US is American, the adjective as readily as the country
the erne is the white-tailed sea eagle and the crossword's standard eagle
Am. is the dictionary's short form of American

annotation.surface: An American eagle spread right across another American's identity papers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'American' is asked for twice and answered two different ways, US the first time and Am. the second. 'All over' is not emphasis: it wraps one piece round another.
annotation.definitionFit: A username is the name you log in under, the string a system knows you by, which is an ID in the everyday sense.

entries.clue: Slight twitching of torso settled (3,4,5)

indicatorNotes.twitching of: A twitching muscle jumps without warning, and the letters this applies to jump out of order in the same way.

blocks.note: a slight is a put-down, a remark meant to belittle
five letters to rearrange

annotation.surface: A small tremor running through somebody's trunk once they had calmed down.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Slight' opens the clue looking like the adjective describing the twitch and is the noun, an insult. The answer is a gardener's metaphor for staying where you are.
annotation.definitionFit: To put down roots is to settle somewhere for good, the way a plant fixes itself into the ground it is in.

entries.clue: Have lovely chat (6)

blocks.note: to have somebody is to con them out of their money
fab is the sixties' word for lovely, short for fabulous

annotation.surface: An invitation to have a pleasant natter.
annotation.walkthrough: Three words and each does a different job, the first two building the answer and the third defining it. 'Have' wants the swindling sense — you were had.
annotation.definitionFit: A confab is an informal talk, short for confabulation, which is a chat with the formality taken out of it.

entries.clue: Sadist periodically traps brown bears (6)

indicatorNotes.periodically: Something done periodically happens at regular intervals rather than all the time, so only every other letter of the word is taken.
indicatorNotes.traps: A trap closes round whatever walks into it, so the letters named here hold the next piece inside them.

blocks.note: the first, third and fifth letters of SaDiSt
tan is the light brown of leather and of sunburnt skin

annotation.surface: A cruel man catching brown bears.
annotation.walkthrough: The bears of the surface are animals; the definition wants the verb, as in bearing pain. Alternate letters can start from either end, and here it is the odd positions that count.
annotation.definitionFit: To stand something is to put up with it — 'I can't stand him' — which is exactly what bearing it means.

entries.clue: Work can be sociable (3,2)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the answer's effect rather than matching it word for word: to opt in is to join in, which is the sociable thing to do.

blocks.note: op is a work, as in a composer's opus number
a tin of beans is a can of beans

annotation.surface: The observation that a job can have a social side to it.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue passes as an office truism, and only the last two words define. 'Can' is the tin on a shelf, and op is the number printed beside a piece in a concert programme.
annotation.definitionFit: To opt in is to choose to take part rather than sit it out, which is the sociable of the two choices.

entries.clue: BLT, Caesar salad? Mayo's capital (9)

indicatorNotes.salad: A salad is a heap of ingredients tossed together in no particular arrangement, which is what becomes of these letters.

blocks.note: nine letters, three of them the sandwich's initials

annotation.surface: A lunch menu offering a bacon sandwich and a Caesar salad, heavy on the mayonnaise.
annotation.walkthrough: Mayo is a county in the west of Ireland as well as the jar on the sandwich counter, and the whole surface exists to keep you thinking about lunch.
annotation.definitionFit: Castlebar is the county town of Mayo, the seat of its council and its largest town, so it is Mayo's capital.

entries.clue: European tied knot in middle of abseil (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition names the continent and the answer one of its nationalities, the usual licence for a national.

indicatorNotes.in: What is in something sits within it, so the letters named before go inside the ones that follow.
indicatorNotes.middle of: The middle of a word is its centre, so only the letters at the heart of it are taken.

blocks.note: abSEil has six letters and these are the middle two
tying the knot is getting wed

annotation.surface: A European who tied a knot halfway down an abseil.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tied knot' is one idea and not two: to tie the knot is to marry. The rope and the cliff are there to make the middle of the abseil sound like a spot on the descent.
annotation.definitionFit: A Swede is somebody from Sweden, which is a European country, so the answer names a European by nationality.

entries.clue: Attractive spies wearing buff and navy perhaps wanting uniform (9)

indicatorNotes.wearing: Whoever wears a coat is inside it, so the letters named before this word sit within the ones around them.
indicatorNotes.perhaps: Perhaps admits that the word beside it is only one instance of what is meant, so the broader word it is an example of is wanted.
indicatorNotes.wanting: A thing wanting something lacks it, so the letter named next is missing from what has been built.

blocks.note: a film buff is a film fan
the CIA is America's foreign intelligence service
navy is one particular shade of blue
U is uniform in the radio alphabet, and it is the letter taken out

annotation.surface: Good-looking agents dressed in buff and navy because no uniform was to be had.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Buff' is the enthusiast and not the colour, though the colours around it work hard to suggest otherwise. Uniform is the radio alphabet's U — alpha, bravo, charlie — and it is the letter that leaves.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody fanciable is somebody you could fancy, the British way of saying you find a person physically attractive.

entries.clue: A little short on gasoline, land in the sea (5)

indicatorNotes.A little: A little of something is a small helping taken out of the middle of it, which is where these letters come from.

blocks.note: shorT ON GAsoline, the letters running straight through two word breaks

annotation.surface: Running low on fuel and coming down in the ocean.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves of the clue describe the same forced landing, so nothing in it points at a country. Hidden answers hide best across word breaks, and this one crosses two.
annotation.definitionFit: Tonga is an archipelago nation in the South Pacific, so its land does literally sit in the sea.

entries.clue: Volcanic rock at the bottom beginning to topple (6)

indicatorNotes.beginning to: The beginning of a word is the letter it opens with, so only that one letter of what follows is wanted.

blocks.note: basal means situated at the base of a thing
the opening letter of topple

annotation.surface: A rock at the foot of a cliff that is starting to fall.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At the bottom' and 'beginning to' both read as position in the surface picture, and only one of them is about position in a word. Basal is the adjective made from base.
annotation.definitionFit: Basalt is the dark fine-grained rock that lava cools into, and it is the commonest volcanic rock on earth.

entries.clue: Big Data Institute's announced acronym for what Big Brother keeps on you (5,3)

annotation.definition: what Big Brother keeps on you

indicatorNotes.acronym: An acronym is built from the opening letters of a name, so those three initials are all that is taken.
indicatorNotes.announced: Announced means read out, so what has been gathered is to be judged by its sound and not by its spelling.

blocks.note: the three initials of the name, in order
say those three letters out loud, bee-dee-eye

annotation.surface: A remark that a data institute's initials happen to name the thing a watcher keeps on you.
annotation.walkthrough: Big Brother is the all-seeing state of Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, and a Big Data Institute is a fair modern stand-in for him. The initials have to be spoken, not read.
annotation.definitionFit: To keep a beady eye on somebody is to watch them closely and suspiciously, which is all Big Brother ever does.
